subject: What Changed to Your Credit Card Today? Edition 12
summary: Axis Bank's Vistara Credit Card gets a hard cutoff date for existing cardholders' spends, two ICICI premium cards quietly narrow lounge-access wording, and IDFC First reworks rewards on three cards.
body_html:
If you're the kind of person who reads the terms page before you sign up for a card, today's a good day for that instinct. Nothing here is a headline-grabbing fee hike, but there's a genuine "your card stops working" notice buried on Axis Bank's Vistara page, a couple of ICICI premium cards quietly narrowing who exactly gets unlimited lounge access, and IDFC First reworking how two of its cards pay you back. None of it is dramatic on its own. All of it is worth five minutes if you hold one of these cards.

One pattern is worth flagging before we go card by card. On more than one ICICI premium card today, the lounge access line quietly picked up the words "for the Primary Cardholder" where it didn't say that before. I can't confirm yet whether this means add-on cardholders are actually losing access, ICICI hasn't announced anything, and it's entirely possible this is just tighter wording for the same benefit. But if you're the primary holder and someone else uses an add-on card on your account for lounge visits, it's worth a call to ICICI to confirm nothing's actually changed for them.

AXIS BANK VISTARA Credit Card

Axis Bank stopped issuing new Vistara Credit Cards a while back, that part isn't news. What's new today is a hard date for existing cardholders: the card will stop working for spends after 31 October 2026, because Vistara itself is merging into Air India. Axis's own language on the page now reads: apply for another Axis Bank Credit Card today to keep uninterrupted access to rewards, offers, and privileges.

There's no ₹ math to run here, the number that matters is a date, not a rupee figure. What you should actually check is how many Vistara Club Miles or Maharaja Points you're sitting on, and whether they'll transfer into Air India's program or need to be redeemed before the cutoff. Airline mergers have a habit of shrinking or resetting loyalty balances during the transition, and Axis's notice doesn't say either way.

The catch: if you hold this card and you're carrying a meaningful points balance, don't wait until October to check. Call Axis or Vistara's frequent flyer desk now and get a straight answer on what happens to your points after the merger, then decide whether to burn them on a booking before 31 October or trust the transition.

Times Black Credit Card

This is one of the two ICICI cards carrying the wording change I flagged above. The old line read like a blanket promise: unlimited complimentary lounge access at domestic and international airports, no cardholder qualifier attached. The new version splits it into two rows, both still unlimited, both now explicitly for the Primary Cardholder.

Nothing here says add-on cardholders have lost access. But the qualifier is new, and it appeared on more than one ICICI card the same day, which is the kind of thing worth confirming rather than assuming away.

The catch: if you've got an add-on card on your Times Black account and someone else uses it for lounge visits, call ICICI and get it in writing that their access is unaffected, before they get turned away at a lounge counter.

Emeralde Credit Card

Same story as Times Black, on the same day. "Get access to international and domestic airport lounges for the primary Cardholder" used to be one line; it's now two, unlimited access to international lounges and unlimited access to domestic lounges, both stated for the Primary Cardholder specifically. Same caveat applies: I haven't found anything confirming add-on cardholders are actually excluded now, this could just be ICICI tightening its own copy.

The catch: same as above. If an add-on cardholder on your account relies on lounge access, confirm with ICICI directly rather than finding out at the airport.

Purchase Credit Card

This is IDFC First's business spending card, and today it lost its old choice between reward points and cash rebates. The page used to advertise 10X reward points on international transactions and 3X on domestic ones, or a rebate option instead. That's gone, replaced by a flat rebate of up to 150 basis points, which is 1.5%, on spends, alongside a long list of merchant categories that now earn nothing at all: utilities, government payments, schools, post office, fuel, agricultural services, property management, transport, contractors, supermarkets, and government healthcare fees.

Run the math on a business doing ₹5 lakh a month in card spend. 1.5% back is ₹7,500 a month, ₹90,000 a year, if every rupee of that spend qualifies. It almost never does. Fuel and utility payments alone are recurring costs for most small businesses, and both are now on the excluded list. If a fifth of your spend sits in those categories, your real rebate drops closer to ₹72,000 a year, not ₹90,000.

The catch: before you assume 1.5% back on everything, pull your last three months of statements and check how much of your actual spend falls into the excluded categories. The number on the page is a ceiling, not what you'll actually earn.

LIC Select

Small but specific change: accelerated reward points on LIC insurance premium payments are now capped at the first five payments in a statement cycle. Pay a sixth LIC premium in the same cycle, on a different policy, say, and it earns only the base rate, no acceleration.

If your household runs multiple LIC policies, term cover for two earning members, an endowment plan, a child plan, this is worth knowing before you assume every premium payment earns the same accelerated rate.

The catch: if you're paying five or more LIC premiums through this card in a single statement cycle, consider spacing a couple of them into the next cycle so they hit the accelerated rate instead of the base one.

LIC Classic

Same change, same day, same bank: the first five LIC premium payments in a statement cycle get accelerated reward points, anything beyond that earns the base rate.

The catch: same fix as LIC Select. If you're close to the five-payment cap, timing which premiums you pay in which cycle can be worth more than it sounds.

What I'd actually do with this

If you hold the Axis Bank Vistara Credit Card, don't wait for October. Call and find out what happens to your points balance after the Air India merger, then decide whether to redeem now or trust the transition.

If someone in your family uses an add-on card on your ICICI Times Black or Emeralde account for lounge access, get written confirmation from ICICI that nothing's changed for them. The new wording gives you a reason to ask, not yet a reason to panic.

If you run a business on the IDFC First Purchase Credit Card, check your actual spend mix against the new exclusion list before you count on 1.5% back across the board.

And if LIC premiums are a recurring feature of your month on either LIC Select or LIC Classic, keep an eye on how many you're paying per statement cycle.

This is my honest read, not formal financial advice. I'm not your advisor, and before you act on anything here, run it past a professional or at least sleep on it. But this is exactly how I'd think about it if these were my cards.

Monzy

items.summary: Card will stop working for spends after 31 October 2026 due to the Vistara-Air India merger; new applicants already couldn't get this card.
Unlimited lounge access wording split into two rows and newly qualified as 'for the Primary Cardholder'; unclear if add-on cardholders are affected.
Same Primary Cardholder wording narrowing as Times Black, applied to its unlimited lounge access lines.
Rewards-or-rebate choice replaced with a flat up to 150bps rebate, and a long list of merchant categories (fuel, utilities, government, etc.) now earn nothing.
Accelerated reward points on LIC premium payments now capped at the first 5 payments per statement cycle.
Same accelerated-points cap as LIC Select: first 5 LIC premium payments per statement cycle only.
